item.title: GOP set to block Trump Pentagon picks as other military moves face headwinds
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senate Republicans are poised to block at least two of President Donald Trump’s nominees for senior Pentagon roles, escalating intense policy disagreements within the GOP, according to current and former officials familiar with the matter. Austin Dahmer and Alex Velez-Green were nominated more than a year ago to become the Pentagon policy office’s director of strategy, plans and capabilities and as the office’s deputy director, respectively. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But despite months of lobbying by the administration, neither has enough votes to advance, and they will not be among a final batch of nominees considered by the Senate this year, those familiar with the matter said. Like others, these people spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the situation. A spokesperson for the Senate Armed Services Committee’s Republican majority did not respond to a request for comment. Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January following their blowout victory in the midterm elections, are not expected to support Dahmer and Velez-Green either, the current and former officials said. With six weeks to go before Republicans lose their majorities on Capitol Hill, the stalled nominations are one of several areas where the Trump administration is encountering obstacles to its priorities for the Pentagon, including its plans for a $1.5 trillion defense budget. The White House is also running out of time to secure Senate confirmation of its picks for Navy secretary and the Army’s top officer. A senior Pentagon official said in an interview that it was possible Dahmer and Velez-Green may be renominated for the same positions next year and that the Defense Department wasn’t ruling out the potential for them to advance in a Democratic-controlled Senate. A White House spokesperson, Olivia Wales, called on Congress to confirm Trump’s nominees “without delay,” but declined to address specific questions for this report. Top Pentagon officials have urged Republicans to use their remaining time in power to pass $350 billion in defense funding through a party-line process that would not require any Democratic support. The money would pay for a range of military equipment, some of which would help the Pentagon recover from the strain on munitions and weapons platforms caused by the administration’s war with Iran. Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg visited Capitol Hill on Wednesday to lobby Republicans on the effort. In a sign that the GOP does not consider such a large sum realistic, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) told reporters afterward that he would first attempt to pass a bipartisan defense spending bill with Democrats. Dahmer and Velez-Green previously served as national security advisers in the Senate. While awaiting confirmation, they have held acting roles as senior deputies to Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby. Velez-Green has helped lead the Pentagon’s review of U.S. military posture in Europe, while Dahmer has helped write high-level strategy documents. Resistance to their nominations began last year amid what has become an acrimonious feud between Colby and congressional Republicans that has come to represent a broader debate within the Republican Party over Trump’s “America First” foreign policy. A year ago, shortly before their confirmation hearings, the Pentagon announced it was withdrawing an Army brigade from Romania despite the objections of GOP defense hawks, who publicly criticized both officials for failing to consult lawmakers before finalizing the decision. As The Washington Post reported in June, House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers (R-Alabama) later accused Colby of lying to him about the withdrawal - an allegation Colby has denied. The stalled confirmations have frustrated officials within the Pentagon exasperated by their inability to reach a deal with Senate Republicans, current and former officials said. At different points this year, staff within the Pentagon policy office suggested that officials from the Baltic nations that border Russia opposed the two nominees and were, in part, responsible for the impasse, according to one current and one former official - who said the allegation was false. The senior Pentagon official said that the administration had heard from multiple sources that Baltic officials had spoken poorly of Dahmer and Velez-Green but that it was unclear how influential those comments were. They also said the Defense Department does not blame the countries for the Senate’s decision to block the nominations. Spokespeople for the Latvian, Lithuanian and Estonian embassies in Washington either did not respond to or declined requests for comment. The Pentagon has instead prioritized the confirmation of other Trump nominees, including Hung Cao, tapped to lead the Navy, and Gen. Chris LaNeve, the administration’s pick for Army chief of staff. Cao encountered bipartisan frustration during his Senate confirmation hearing this week, as lawmakers vented about the Trump administration’s responsiveness to Congress and its desire to replace the electromagnetic catapults that launch fighters from aircraft carriers with older steam-powered systems - a change that could cost billions of dollars. “Returning to steam is a nonstarter and everybody needs to understand that,” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), the Senate Armed Services Committee chair, told Cao during the hearing. Because he only recently retired from the Navy, Cao will require a 60-vote waiver in the Senate to be confirmed as the service’s next civilian leader. Multiple Democrats on the committee said after the hearing that they will oppose his confirmation. Trump appointed Cao the Navy’s acting secretary after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pushed out Cao’s predecessor, billionaire John Phelan, in April. LaNeve, the Army’s vice chief of staff, was made the service’s acting military leader after Hegseth fired the job’s former occupant, Gen. Randy George. Hegseth has declined to explain why he fired George, despite facing questions from Republicans and Democrats supportive of the ousted general. As The Post reported in August, LaNeve urged George shortly before his firing to drop an internal investigation into whether Army helicopter pilots broke regulations by flying past country musician Kid Rock’s Nashville home. Hegseth later ended the investigation himself, posting a message on social media in support of the soldiers involved in the flyby. Some Republicans have privately opposed LaNeve’s nomination, which has been delayed for months despite Hegseth urging the White House to formally tap him for the role, current and former officials said. Trump did so Tuesday. Sen. Joni Ernst (Iowa), a retiring Republican who has opposed LaNeve’s confirmation, said that she would “love to see this work out” but that a successful outcome was “probably up to the administration.” The Army has no Senate-confirmed service secretary either. The job is currently held on an acting basis by Adam Telle. His predecessor, Dan Driscoll, resigned after repeated clashes with Hegseth. The Trump administration has not yet announced its nominee to permanently lead the service. item.title: Jan. 6 leader who once backed Trump now says he's 'absolutely done'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
IRVING, Texas (AP) — Stewart Rhodes didn’t just go to prison for Donald Trump . While serving time for his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, the founder of the right-wing militia known as the Oath Keepers got a tattoo of Trump’s defiant face after he survived an assassin’s bullet in Butler, Pennsylvania . It was further proof of Rhodes' devotion to the Republican president. But that's all over now. “I am absolutely done with Trump,” said Rhodes, sitting at a rickety yellow table outside a gastropub in Irving, Texas. He considers Trump not just a traitor, but "one of the very worst in our nation's history.” The repudiation from a former acolyte — one convicted of seditious conspiracy for orchestrating an ill-fated attempt to keep Trump in power six years ago — is another example of how allegiance to the president has faded even among extreme supporters. Back then, Rhodes claimed Trump lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden because of election fraud. This year in Texas, where Democrats had historic victories , he said there's another reason. “The lion’s share is because Trump pissed off his own base," Rhodes said, his face shaded by a black cowboy hat. An eye patch covers his left socket, the result of an old gun accident, and a glacial blue iris peers out from the other. Nearby, people mingled with drinks for his Christian Warriors After-Party, organized during a three-day conference called “Christ is King: America After Trump.” Some people approached to shake hands or sign up for the Oath Keepers or trainings for things like community defense and hurricane relief. ‘The first inkling’ of a split from Trump The beginning of Rhodes' break with Trump came when the president gave pardons to hundreds of people who were locked up for their actions on Jan. 6, 2021, but only commuted Rhodes' sentence . “That was the first inkling,” Rhodes said. Rhodes also said Trump's war with Iran violated Trump's promises to end foreign conflicts. And, Rhodes said, it felt like an affront when Trump dismissed people who urged his administration to release files about the Jeffrey Epstein case , calling them “PAST supporters.” Then Rhodes felt Trump went back on his longtime slogan. “We elected him to end the corruption in Washington, D.C. ‘Drain the swamp.’ Unfortunately his administration has been one of the most corrupt administrations in U.S. history," Rhodes said. “The pardons are pay-for-play and everything is pay-for-play.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Rhodes is not alone in his about-face on Trump, but there's an ideological through line, said Sam Jackson, an associate professor at the University at Albany with a focus on anti-government extremism. “They went from seeing Donald Trump as their ally in this fight against the conspiracy, to actually being co-opted by the conspiracy,” Jackson said, and it “points to deeper consistency in that understanding of the world as driven by hidden, evil actors.” Rhodes, who graduated from Yale Law School and worked for former U.S. Rep. Ron Paul of Texas, founded the Oath Keepers in 2009 with the goal of encouraging members of the military and law enforcement to resist what they view as unconstitutional orders, such as disarming citizens or carrying out warrantless searches. Watching from prison when Trump was fired on Rhodes later allied himself with Trump's political movement, and the Oath Keepers supported his attempt to remain in office after losing the 2020 election. Fueled with conspiracies about voter fraud, prosecutors said group members gathered weapons, organized trainings and assembled in Washington , where some helped storm the Capitol on Jan. 6. Rhodes, who did not enter the building that day, said he was a “political prisoner" who faced “illegality” in his trial. He was sentenced to 18 years, one of the longest sentences of any Jan. 6 case. “You are smart, you are charismatic and compelling and frankly that’s what makes you dangerous,” U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta said during the hearing. “The moment you are released, whenever that may be, you will be ready to take up arms against your government.” Rhodes was behind bars as Trump began his political comeback. He said he watched the assassination attempt in Butler on a prison television with other inmates. He saw Trump pump his fist and yell “fight,” and he figured that God’s hand was on the man. After Trump won the 2024 election, he swiftly pardoned hundreds of people convicted of crimes related to Jan. 6, including those who assaulted police officers. Rhodes received a commutation, which didn’t wipe his record clean. “He let us out of prison. We were grateful. I didn’t get a pardon though,” he said. Tattoo that honored Trump will be ‘modified’ to reflect a new reality The Justice Department vacated Rhodes' conviction earlier this year, lifting his felon status. Rhodes said he's working to rebuild the Oath Keepers, which previously had tens of thousands of members, according to leaked lists. With his rights restored, Rhodes said his first priority was to get some guns, and he didn't register to vote in time for the election. But he said he wouldn't have cast a ballot anyway. That's because Rhodes felt that “the Republican Party has taken us for granted," and he didn't want to choose between “a half a dose of poison or a full dose.” As for his tattoo of Trump, the man he now considers a traitor, Rhodes has plans that he didn't specify. “I will have this prison tattoo of Trump ‘modified,'” he wrote in a text message, “to reflect that reality. That treason.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/oath-keepers-founder-jan-6-130043975.html

item.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks have increased to highest level since Iran war began
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Reported attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been higher in number in October and November than any previous months since the war between the U.S., Israel and Iran began in late February , according to data compiled by maritime organizations. The attacks appear to be a bid to complicate U.S.-led efforts to keep oil flowing through the economically crucial Strait of Hormuz despite an Iranian-declared blockade, experts told ABC News. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 31 attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October, and about 19 in November, as of Nov. 18. Noppadon Wongsuvan via AP Photo - PHOTO: Smoke billows from the Mayuree Naree, a Thailand-flagged bulk carrier, after it was hit by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, north of Oman, on March 11, 2026. Previously, a total of 53 incidents had been reported to the UKMTO between March and September of this year, averaging 10 to 15 incidents total across both Strait of Hormuz and surrounding gulfs in previous months. The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a United Nations agency, has slightly more conservative numbers, with 34 attacks confirmed in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October and November so far. This too, is still a marked increase from previous numbers the IMO had collected, which number roughly 50 in and around the Strait of Hormuz between March and September. The IMO has tallied 138 attacks on vessels in total across the Middle East since the war began. The positions of attacked tankers reported to the UKMTO indicate that most attacked vessels were in the very southern portion of the Strait of Hormuz, staying close to the Omani coastline, according to the maritime group's data. Social media via Reuters - PHOTO: Smoke rises at sea off the coast of Oman, Nov. 18, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. What experts say Iran aims to accomplish "Iran's objective remains to keep the Omani route, which is described as a U.S.-facilitated route, a very high-risk passage and to keep the energy recovery inconsistent," Noam Raydan, senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told ABC News. Felt Maps/UKMTO/Verified UGC - PHOTO: Map identifying locations where vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October and November of 2026, according to UKMTO data. "Washington and its regional partners have found ways to keep oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told ABC News. "Tehran now seems determined to make these arrangements more costly and less reliable." The workaround developed by the U.S. involves "ship-to-ship" (STS) transfers in which smaller tankers cross the strait with tracking systems switched off, and transfer cargos to larger tankers once safely on the other side, Sina Toossi, senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, told ABC News. Iran is now responding in "a cycle of adaptation and counter-adaptation," he said. "Tehran has escalated its attacks to make the STS system more dangerous, costly, and ultimately unviable. Iran's broader objective is to demonstrate that normal oil exports cannot continue while the US maintains its blockade of Iran, and to generate enough economic pressure to force Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict," Toossi said. The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade, stopping Iranian and Iran-linked ships from going in and out of the Gulf of Oman, starting April 13, with a brief pause from June 18 to July 13. Anadolu via Getty Images - PHOTO: Commercial vessels and oil tankers sit anchored in the waters off Bandar Abbas in southern Iran's Hormozgan Province on Sept. 9, 2026. Attacks not isolated to ships crossing the strait Strikes have not been limited to ships. On Nov. 8, Iran attacked the Omani island of Didamar in the strait itself, according to satellite images and video verified by ABC News. The island hosts radar and satellite communications technology. Iranian state media said Iran had struck what it described as "enemy navigation aid systems." Oman, a U.S. partner, did not comment on the attack. Copernicus Sentinel 2 - PHOTO: Satellite image of Oman's Didamar island in the Strait of Hormuz following claimed Iranian attacks on infrastructure on the island. Strikes have also not been isolated to ships actively crossing the strait. ABC News has verified at least one incident in which a ship was attacked by a drone appearing to belong to Iran, despite not making any attempt to cross the strait. In early October, the Panama-flagged supertanker Gem No. 2 had been idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in the Persian Gulf, outside the Strait of Hormuz, for nearly five months. It was fully loaded with a cargo of two million barrels of Saudi crude oil, per maritime intelligence company Kpler, and was one of the hundreds of ships the International Maritime Organization estimates is stuck in the Persian Gulf since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. What happened to Gem No. 2? Two crew members who were on board Gem No. 2 say the ship never attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz, and that it was attacked by one drone on Oct. 9 and then at least three others on Oct. 10, the latter attack sparking a massive fire and forcing the ship's evacuation, according to videos filmed by the crew obtained and verified by ABC News. Obtained by ABC News - PHOTO: Oil Tanker Gem No2 on fire after being hit by drones while sitting idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in October 2026. Hours after the vessel was struck for a second time and evacuated, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in an online post that the vessel had struck a naval mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route. Satellite images taken in the days after it was abandoned confirm Gem No. 2's position off the coast of the UAE, well outside the Strait of Hormuz. Copernicus Sentinel 2 - PHOTO: Satellite image of oil tanker Gem No2 off the coast of the UAE on October 24, two weeks after being attacked. ABC News showed images taken by the crew of the wreckage of the drone that struck the ship on Oct. 9 to Fabian Hinz, a researcher who studies drone warfare. Hinz said the wreckage in the images belongs to a jet-powered Hadid-110, built by Iran. Iran continues to say the ship hit a mine. Large tankers targeted: Analyst Azizi, the ICG's Iran analyst, suggested that "large oil tankers seem to be receiving particular attention, whether they are moving through the strait or operating elsewhere in the Persian Gulf." "One possible explanation is that Tehran wants to discourage the use of supertankers and prevent the development of alternative shipping arrangements that could make the blockade less effective," he said. Obtained by ABC News - PHOTO: Pieces of a drone that hit oil tanker Gem No2 on October 9th, identified as an Iranian Hadid-110 drone by an expert to ABC News. It's not clear why Gem No. 2 was allegedly targeted, but the vessel would have been an easy target, according to Samir Madani, co-founder of TankerTrackers.c o m . Madani told ABC News he noticed Gem No. 2 before the attack because the tanker's location transmission services were turned on, revealing its location publicly. Both Azizi and Toossi describe Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz as having "strategic logic." "Ultimately, the objective goes beyond disrupting oil exports. Iran is trying to demonstrate that the United States cannot guarantee maritime security in the Persian Gulf despite its overwhelming naval superiority," Azizi told ABC News. Toossi added that this strategy will have consequences far beyond the strait. "The danger is that this escalating contest will produce a much wider disruption of regional shipping and energy infrastructure, with even greater consequences for the global economy," he said. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/International/strait-hormuz-attacks-increased-highest-level-iran-war/story?id=138304456

item.title: Anthropic engineer proposes a theory for all these outages
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
There have been so many prominent tech services experiencing outages lately that the problems have gone mainstream in a new way we haven't seen before. Besides the headlines and podcasts (some of which are asking if this is actually a new thing or if we're just noticing it more), the tech outages have kept Vice President JD Vance from attending New York events , led to the resignation of the White House's cybersecurity chief , made “Saturday Night Live,” and been the subject of tons of memes and TikTok comedy where people joke that "LinkedIn and Tinder must be down, because I'm not getting any responses!" As we wrote recently , the problems are far more than just cybersecurity, though AI means hackers can discover and exploit bugs like never before. Infrastructure is decrepit. Maintenance is deferred. Exhausted, too-small teams of IT workers aren't up to this level of chaos. But there's another explanation that's perhaps underappreciated: one big downside of Claude Code, the marquee product that has given Anthropic ( ANT ) its trillion-dollar valuation. The problem is best explained by someone who would know best: a prominent Anthropic engineer (and former Google engineer) who works on Claude Code as a member of the technical staff, Addy Osmani, whose treatise on " comprehension debt " bounced around the software engineering community in March — and is even more relevant today. What Osmani highlights isn't really a weakness in Claude Code, but in how companies and engineering teams use it. The gist: AI can write code faster than we can review it. The speed is a great benefit, but it's also a curse, as myriad companies pivot from writing code to overseeing teams of AI agents that complain less and write more. As Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week , the company's engineers "build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product." Dario Amodei is seen on the display at the Nasdaq MarketSite as shares of Anthropic begin trading after their IPO in Times Square, New York City, United States, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Stephanie Keith/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto via Getty Images Traditionally, the laborious process of checking other people's code is how software engineers internalize why systems are designed the way they are, and why decisions from earlier in a project might be meaningful today. But reviewing the entirety of AI code isn't feasible given how fast we can produce it now. It's too unwieldy, and this represents a massive bottleneck for progress. Tests, AI review, and spending less time reviewing can be effective. But they've removed layers of verification, and ultimately comprehension, which is disappearing, Osmani explains. All this means that with code piling up faster than humans can review it, companies can lose control of their systems in a way far more prosaic and banal than some sort of sentient AI or Skynet doomsday scenario. With human code proofreaders at their limits, when things inevitably break , that missing understanding matters. Coders — or even AI — may not realize that a few lines of code represent an important piece of figurative duct tape, a load-bearing wall, or a mechanism that triggers other contingencies. Every patch or attempted fix can also break more things. That brings us back to the wave of cyber outages . Aside from a few high-profile lawsuits and public scandals, the tech giants whose software "ate the world" and that now commandeer our attention spans have largely escaped meaningful accountability. Their software failures are embarrassing. And their design choices have led to allegations of addiction, anti-social behavior, and economic exploitation. But they have, generally speaking, escaped rigorous regulation. AI changes the calculus. The era of honor system self-policing may be coming to an end. "When AI-generated code is running in healthcare systems, financial infrastructure, and government services," Osmani wrote, the excuse that an AI wrote bad code and we didn't fully review it "will not hold up in a post-incident report when lives or significant assets are at stake." Cyber outages are often a nuisance and, mercifully, haven't led to a mass-casualty event or prolonged economic crisis. But in a world where AI can generate code faster than anyone can keep up, it's not hard to imagine that changing. By Nate Raymond Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US House of Representatives unconstitutionally passed a $1.7 trillion government funding bill in 2022 through a pandemic-era rule allowing lawmakers to vote by ‌proxy rather than in person, a federal appeals court ruled on Friday. The New Orleans-based ‌5th US Circuit Court of Appeals voted 9-8 to uphold an injunction that outgoing Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton ​secured blocking enforcement of a provision of that measure that gave pregnant workers stronger legal protections. Democrat Nancy Pelosi, the speaker of the House at the time, helped implement the proxy voting rule in May 2020 following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic as an emergency measure. The rule was ditched when ‌Republicans took control of the House ⁠after the November 2022 elections. Before Republicans took control, the House used the proxy voting rule to pass a spending package that included the provision Paxton challenged, ⁠called the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. It was signed into law by Democratic President Joe Biden. The bill passed the House on a 225-201 vote, with 226 members voting by proxy. Friday's ruling, powered by the 5th ​Circuit's ​conservative majority, held that the proxy rule violated the ​US Constitution's quorum clause, which the court ‌said requires a majority of House members to be physically present to pass legislation. "While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat," wrote US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump. While the decision concerns how the entire bill was passed, the relief that ‌the 5th Circuit granted Paxton's office was narrow, as it ​barred the US Department of Justice and the Equal ​Employment Opportunity Commission from enforcing the pregnant ​workers provision against Texas. The DOJ, which defended the law, and Paxton's office did ‌not respond to requests for comment. US Circuit ​Judge James Graves, an appointee ​of Democratic President Barack Obama, in a dissenting opinion called the ruling "illogical, inexplicable, and invalid." He said the majority read a physical-presence requirement into the quorum clause that does not ​exist. Graves said the majority provided ‌no explanation for why, if the entirety of the law was unconstitutionally passed, its ​ruling "should be limited only to one small sliver of the multitrillion dollar bill." item.title: Bayer agrees to pay up to $7.25 billion over Roundup cancer claims spanning decades
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge. The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness. For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users. Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements. Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling. In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are “fair and adequate” and the total dollar amount is “among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.” The approved settlement includes $600 million for attorneys' fees. The judge said there was a risk Bayer would have filed for bankruptcy protection if the settlement had been rejected. Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation." The decision could be appealed. Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer’s deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less. The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens. Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as “probably carcinogenic” in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it’s not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed. About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets. The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion. In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court’s precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict “should send a strong signal” that plaintiffs “will face significant challenges” pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer’s U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader. Attorneys disagree on whether the settlement is fair Bayer previously set aside $16 billion to cover legal costs related to Roundup cases. The new settlement, which is in addition to that, is designed to address most of the remaining lawsuits, as well as any additional cases brought in the coming years by people who were exposed to Roundup before the settlement was proposed in February. “Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case. The settlement calls for Bayer to make annual payments into a special fund for up to 21 years, totaling as much as $7.25 billion. The amount of money paid out to individuals would vary. Agricultural, industrial or turf workers exposed at length to Roundup could receive an average of $165,000 if they were diagnosed with an aggressive form of the illness while younger than age 60. But anyone diagnosed at age 78 or older would get significantly less, with an average of $10,000. Some attorneys have said the individual settlement amounts are too small and the terms too restrictive. “This settlement is the scariest, worst future settlement that’s ever been contemplated,” attorney Gerson Smoger said during a September court hearing on whether the settlement was fair. He said it locked in future claimants for decades with no chance at punitive damages yet “kept the product that they were exposed to on the market, allowing the victims to continue to be exposed.” The settlement was filed in St. Louis Circuit Court in Missouri, home to Bayer’s North America crop science division and the state where many of the lawsuits have been brought. item.title: More trouble for Nvidia as SEC reportedly probes accounting amid historic stock slide
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books. Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss, before bouncing nearly 4% in after-hours trading. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment. The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $490 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ). Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee. Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China. Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on. Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership . California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said. The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market. Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report. "Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday. item.title: DOJ turns attention to Democratic operatives in Alaska Senate election probe
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Alaska Democratic Senator-elect Mary Peltola looks on during a midterm election night watch party in Anchorage, Alaska, on November 3. - Justin Sullivan/Getty Images/File With Alaska’s Senate race now called, the Justice Department is shifting focus toward Sen.-elect Mary Peltola’s campaign as part of its ongoing criminal investigation into an alleged scheme to run a spoiler candidate against her opponent, according to two people familiar with the matter. The focus marks a shift in the investigation, which thrust the Justice Department into the center of a contentious political race. For months, investigators had focused on whether former candidate Daniel J. Sullivan intended to siphon votes from Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, whose name is similar. Just before the election, however, a New York Times report described an alleged coordinated effort involving the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) to improve her chances of victory. Peltola has publicly said she was not aware of the alleged effort. With public pressure from President Donald Trump and from Justice Department headquarters, some officials weighed whether a possible charge could be brought against the alleged spoiler candidate nicknamed “Decoy Dan,” according to one of the people familiar with the discussions. The investigation has since shifted away from Daniel J. Sullivan and is now focused on Peltola’s campaign, the DSCC and outside political consultants allegedly involved in the scheme, another person familiar with the matter said. The Justice Department also has sent dozens of FBI agents to Alaska and issued hundreds of subpoenas and preservation letters as part of the probe, that person said. Gerald Heikes , a longshot candidate, was issued a subpoena as part of a DOJ probe, CNN previously reported. More than a dozen people have received letters saying they may be targets of the investigation, CNN has reported. Democrats have denounced the investigation as politically motivated, arguing that recruiting spoiler candidates is a common and legal strategy. Meanwhile, the Justice Department has moved to drop its lawsuit seeking to block certification of Peltola’s victory. The suit argued that certification should be delayed while an investigation determined whether voters had been confused. A judge rejected the Justice Department’s longshot certification delay effort before Election Day, a move that hinged on whether the margin of Peltola’s victory was larger than the number of votes Daniel J. Sullivan received. The official count shows that even if Daniel J. Sullivan’s votes were counted for Sen. Sullivan, Peltola would still win. Two days after the race was decided, the administration asked a court to declare the case moot. CNN has reached out to the Peltola campaign and the DSCC for comment.
